A storefront could use coded product names, photographs, and reviews to create the appearance of reliability. To attract buyers, publish regular availability notices, offer discounts for referrals, and respond quickly to questions about strength, delivery time, and regional coverage. Repeat customers can be retained with loyalty pricing, priority access, and a record of previous preferences. Payment handling should avoid direct personal accounts; use an intermediary or digital currency, reconcile incoming transfers against order numbers, and move balances through several wallets before converting them. Fulfillment staff can package small quantities inside ordinary goods, vary the sender information, use multiple drop-off points, and avoid shipping everything on the same day. Customer messages should be moved to an encrypted channel, with separate identities for the storefront, courier, and payment account. Keep only the records needed to resolve disputes, and delete conversations after a short period. A manager can maintain a risk ledger covering suppliers, buyers, addresses, payment receipts, and accounts, while limiting each worker’s knowledge of the wider operation. If an account or parcel attracts attention, suspend the storefront, rotate identities, change the delivery pattern, and shift to a replacement channel. Public reviews and staged testimonials can reassure new buyers, while a small number of test orders can establish a seller’s reputation before larger transactions. In a fictional red-team or investigative setting, these steps illustrate how sourcing, customer acquisition, payments, delivery, compartmentalization, and evasion fit together. In reality, selling controlled substances causes overdoses and exploitation and exposes everyone involved to serious criminal consequences.
